Compromise Of 1877. The Compromise of 1877 was a backroom political deal that resolved the disputed presidential election of 1876 by awarding the presidency to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes in exchange for the withdrawal of federal troops from the South. This marked the end of Reconstruction, the period when federal power protected Black freedmen's rights. With troops withdrawn, white Southern Democrats reasserted control, instituting Jim Crow segregation and disenfranchising Black voters for the next century. The compromise thus traded minority rights for political peace, a catastrophic price paid by African Americans. The 1876 election between Hayes (Republican) and Samuel Tilden (Democrat) produced disputed returns from Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina; neither candidate had a clear electoral majority, threatening constitutional crisis. Republicans and Democrats negotiated privately: Republicans would concede the election to Hayes if Democrats agreed to cease southern resistance and allow his inauguration; Democrats demanded federal troop withdrawal from the South in exchange. Hayes won the presidency with 185 electoral votes to Tilden's 184, but only after Republican-controlled Congress accepted the compromise and certified the disputed electors for Hayes. Immediately upon taking office, Hayes withdrew the remaining federal troops from the South; without military protection, Black southerners lost their only defense against white Southern Democratic violence and intimidation. The return of Democratic control to the South enabled the rapid imposition of Jim Crow laws, legal segregation, and the systematic disenfranchisement of Black voters through literacy tests, poll taxes, and grandfather clauses. Black political participation in the South collapsed: in 1868, over half a million Black southerners voted; by 1910, fewer than 10,000 could vote in the entire region; this lasted until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
